objective: Determining how a change in strategic goals impacts the portfolio and its components
secondaryObjectives: Creating and evaluating what-if portfolio scenarios (options analysis, risk analysis, SWOT, financial analysis)
Recommending a portfolio scenario and its components, with rationale, for governance decision-making
Balancing and prioritizing portfolio components to optimize resource utilization against strategic objectives

sources.cite: PMI, Portfolio Management Professional (PfMP) Examination Content Outline (PRA-206-2017, July 2017): Strategic Alignment 25%, Governance 20%, Portfolio Performance 25%, Portfolio Risk Management 15%, Communications Management 15%
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch of a copy of PMI's PDF hosted by a training provider. Relevant text: Strategic Alignment Task 5 scenarios 'in order to evaluate and select viable options'; Task 6 'Recommend portfolio scenario(s) and related components, based on prioritization analysis/criteria'; Task 7 'Determine the impact to portfolio and portfolio components due to changes in strategic goals and objectives'; Portfolio Performance Task 6 'Balance portfolio and prioritize portfolio components, using established criteria and methods'; Task 7 'Analyze and optimize the consolidated allocation/reallocation of capacity'; Governance Task 5 'Make recommendations and obtain approval regarding portfolio decisions'. Whether PMI has a newer outline was not checked. The objective wording is the course seed's.
The water utility, its portfolio, the components' costs and scores, the scenarios and the support gauges are fictional teaching figures for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You are the portfolio manager at Cedar Valley Water, a fictional regional water utility. After two drought years and a regulator's order, the board has changed the strategy: cut water loss from 24% to 15% in three years. Customer growth, which ranked the current portfolio, is now third. Six components share this year's 40 million dollar budget.
handover: Components: smart meters (12 million), new billing system (10), reservoir intake upgrade (7), customer app redesign (6), leak detection pilot (3), office move (2).
The portfolio governance board decides on starting, pausing or stopping components and moving money between them. You analyze, recommend and run the portfolio.
howItWorks: The board shows the portfolio's risks against the appetite, each executive's support in words, the budget committed and the docket.
Move on two weeks at a time. A decision comes to you at each review; before the first you can read the strategy or analyze the dependencies.
After week 10 you write the portfolio record and a short reflection.

effects.finding: New criteria: water-loss reduction (weight 40%), regulatory compliance (25%), financial return (20%), customer experience (15%). The order requires monthly reporting of metered water loss from next year.

effects.log: You map what each component needs from the others.

effects.finding: Smart meters produce interval data only the new billing system can take, and the regulator's monthly report comes from billing. Leak detection needs four data engineers; the four available sit on the app team.

then.log: Week 10: the first 20,000 smart meters go live, and their reads cannot be billed or sent to the regulator: the old billing system cannot take interval data. A stopgap costs 4 million dollars.
Week 10: leak detection is a month behind for want of data engineers.

else.log: Week 10: the first quarter's portfolio report is due.

effects.log: Week 2: the first review after the board's decision.
Week 6: the governance board meets on Thursday.

impactPrompt.title: Week 2: what does the new goal do to the portfolio?
impactPrompt.context: The board's new goal: water loss from 24% to 15% in three years, under a regulator's order. Customer growth, the old first priority, is now third. The six components were ranked on the old criteria: the customer app (6 million) and the office move (2 million) ranked first and second.

choices.label: Re-score all six components against the board's new criteria with their owners, and set out the impact on each one before anything changes

effects.log: Re-scored: smart meters and leak detection now rank first; the app falls to fifth.

choices.feedback: A change in strategic goals is assessed for its impact on every component against the new criteria before decisions are made.

choices.label: Carry on as planned; the components are already approved and funded

effects.log: The portfolio keeps its old ranking.

choices.feedback: Approved components can stop being aligned when the strategy changes; that is what the impact assessment is for.

choices.label: Cancel the app and the office move now; they no longer fit

effects.log: You stop two approved components on your own decision.

choices.feedback: Stopping components is a portfolio decision for the governance board, after analysis.

scenPrompt.title: Week 4: options for the board
scenPrompt.context: The CEO has a favorite: put everything into smart meters. Finance can model costs and returns for any scenario this week; operations can say what capacity each needs.

choices.label: Build three what-if scenarios (A: meters first; B: accelerate leak detection and pause the app; C: cancel billing to fund meters faster) and evaluate each on value against the new criteria, risk, cost and capacity

effects.log: Scenario B scores best: the highest water-loss reduction for the money, within capacity once the app is paused. C saves 10 million but the dependency analysis shows the meters need the new billing system.

choices.feedback: What-if scenarios are evaluated on the prioritization criteria with risk, financial and capacity analysis to select viable options.

choices.label: Work up the CEO's scenario only
choices.feedback: One scenario gives the board no options to weigh.

choices.label: Re-order the list by judgment and skip the scenario work
choices.feedback: A ranking without analysis gives the board no basis for a decision.

recPrompt.title: Week 6: the recommendation
recPrompt.context: The portfolio governance board meets on Thursday. Its charter gives it the decision on starting, pausing or stopping components and on moving money between them.

choices.label: Recommend scenario B to the board with the rationale (water-loss reduction per dollar, the billing dependency, capacity) and record its decision

effects.log: The board approves scenario B: leak detection accelerated, the app paused, billing kept.

choices.feedback: A recommended scenario with its rationale goes to the governance body that holds the decision rights.

choices.label: Put scenario B in place now and brief the board afterward; it is clearly right

effects.log: You pause the app and move its money before the board meets.

choices.feedback: Even the right decision, taken outside the governance model, is a decision without authority.

choices.label: Recommend scenario C: cancel the billing system and put its 10 million into meters

effects.log: The board approves scenario C on your recommendation.

choices.feedback: Cancelling a component that others depend on, without the dependency in the analysis, moves the risk rather than the goal.

reallocPrompt.title: Week 8: who does the leak detection work?
reallocPrompt.context: Leak detection needs four data engineers this month. Four sit on the paused app team, whose manager wants to keep them together for the app's restart next year. Contractors would cost 3 million dollars.

choices.label: Move the four engineers from the paused app to leak detection under the approved scenario, update the roadmap and tell the app team when it restarts

effects.log: Leak detection starts on time; the roadmap shows the app's restart in the new year.

choices.feedback: Capacity is reallocated to the components the approved scenario prioritizes, and the roadmap and the people are updated.

choices.label: Keep the app team together and let leak detection wait for hiring
choices.feedback: Keeping capacity on a paused component starves the one the strategy now puts first.

choices.label: Hire contractors for 3 million dollars and keep the app team together

effects.log: Contractors hired over the committed budget.

choices.feedback: Buying capacity outside the budget when approved capacity is idle is not balancing the portfolio.

reflection.question: Write the note to the board: what the strategy change did to the portfolio, which scenario you recommended and why, and how capacity was rebalanced.

parts.label: Impact and scenarios
parts.criteria: Re-scores the components against the new criteria, and evaluates more than one scenario on value, risk, cost, capacity and dependencies.
parts.modelAnswer: On the new criteria meters and leak detection rank first and the app falls to fifth. Of three scenarios, B gives the most water-loss reduction per dollar within capacity; C saves 10 million but breaks the meters' dependency on billing.

parts.label: Decision and rebalancing
parts.criteria: The recommendation went to the governance board with its rationale; capacity moved from the paused component to the prioritized one, within the budget, and the roadmap was updated.
parts.modelAnswer: The board approved B. The four data engineers moved from the paused app to leak detection, the roadmap shows the app's restart, and spend stayed at 40 million.

authority.body: Starting, pausing and stopping components belong to the governance board; the portfolio manager assesses, evaluates scenarios and recommends.

scoring.modelReasoning: A change in strategic goals is assessed for its impact on every component against the new prioritization criteria. Viable options come from what-if scenarios evaluated on value, risk, cost, capacity and dependencies: cancelling billing looks cheap until the meters' dependency on it is in the analysis. The portfolio manager recommends a scenario with its rationale; the governance board, which holds the decision rights, approves it. Capacity is then reallocated to the prioritized components, here from the paused app, within the budget, and the roadmap is updated.
